flashcard_questions.q: Which refrain ends several stanzas of Owen’s Exposure?
What does that refrain reveal about the soldiers’ situation?
flashcard_questions.a: They wait for an attack that never comes and die of cold instead.

flashcard_questions.q: Which verb makes the east winds a deliberate, violent attacker?
Which technique makes the snowflakes seem predatory in Exposure?
flashcard_questions.a: Personification — they come ‘feeling for our faces’.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Owen call the soldiers as they imagine going home?
Which metaphor shows the people at home as cold and indifferent?
Which rhyme type creates unease throughout Exposure?
Which 1966 collection contains Heaney’s Storm on the Island?
Which government seat is hidden in the first eight letters of Heaney’s title?
Which word for a volley of gunfire does Heaney use for space?
Which simile describes the spray hitting the windows?
flashcard_questions.a: It spits ‘like a tame cat turned savage’.

flashcard_questions.q: Which oxymoron closes Storm on the Island?
Which verse form does Heaney use for the poem’s single stanza?
Why does Heaney write the poem as one unbroken stanza?
flashcard_questions.a: It mirrors the relentless storm, offering no shelter or pause.

flashcard_questions.q: Which opening line shows the islanders’ confidence before the storm?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘We are prepared: we build our houses squat.’

notes: 15 cards across both poems, 7 on Exposure and 8 on Storm on the Island: 6 quotation-recall fronts, 4 quotation-to-technique (‘knive’, personification, the oxymoron, the tame-cat simile), 3 structure-and-form (half-rhyme, blank verse, the single stanza), 2 context cards (Death of a Naturalist, the Stormont title). The existing ‘which Owen poem’ and 1917–18 cards were not repeated. ‘Propaganda’, ‘alliteration’, ‘allegory’ and ‘semantic field’ dropped as glossary restatements that would interfere with the technique cards kept. All quotations verbatim from the lesson content.
